speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Just last week, my Ministry launched Singapore's inaugural Zero Waste Masterplan, a critical achievement in this Year Towards Zero Waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This is a limited print edition of the Masterplan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: In the spirit of Zero Waste, Members can access the Masterplan on our Towards Zero Waste website, too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Masterplan draws on ideas and contributions from a vast array of our population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Masterplan also marks an important milestone in Singapore's sustainable development journey over the last five decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Back in the 1970s, my family wrapped our household waste in newspapers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Food waste was manually collected in little buckets outside our homes and used as swill in our farms and, in return, we received some eggs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: I am not sure how many people in this House remember that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: From time to time, we experienced the waft of interesting odours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Waste disposal is clean and hygienic, and we make use of pneumatic technology to convey waste from our chutes to a collection point for subsequent disposal. "Clean and Green" has become synonymous with Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: And we have also demonstrated that environmental protection can co-exist with economic growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Indeed, we were ranked Asia's most sustainable city in the 2018 Sustainability Cities Index and second in the 2018 World Economic Forum's Global Competitiveness Index.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We have come a long way, but we must do more to ensure that the next generation continues to enjoy a liveable and sustainable home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Doing our part for the environment is even more critical now as we seek to address climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Someone has said that we should never argue about climate change – it always turns into a "heated debate", if you pardon the pun.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: As highlighted by the Prime Minister in his recent National Day Rally Speech, climate change is undoubtedly a massive existential challenge confronting our next generation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: To tackle climate change, we need a paradigm shift from the "take-make-throw" linear model to the circular economy where resources are used over and over again.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Efficient waste disposal is necessary, but our goal must, first and foremost, be to reduce, reuse and recycle; in other words, zero waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This is the core of the Resource Sustainability Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: What we produce, consume and throw away all have an impact on the climate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We must, therefore, change our current patterns of production and consumption to reduce emissions and limit global warming.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Our zero waste efforts will play a key role.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: They will help cut down on carbon intensive activities along the supply chain and reduce the amount of heat-trapping emissions we put into the atmosphere.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Global economic growth is driving resource consumption at an unsustainable rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Studies show that we are at the limits of Planet Earth’s ability to fulfil our resource needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Take lithium, for instance, which is used in batteries for electric cars, laptops and smartphones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Demand for lithium has tripled in the last decade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Companies which rely on lithium to make batteries, along with cobalt and nickel, warn of impending shortages of such critical materials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: If we do not change our habits, there will simply not be enough resources to sustain our way of life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We must address the existential threats of climate change, especially rising sea levels, and cope with rising temperatures and extreme rainfall patterns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We are building up our knowledge of climate science to guide our actions to protect Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We are also stepping up efforts to reduce carbon emissions and mitigate climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Apart from how we transform our industry, transport and energy sectors to pursue sustainable production and consumption, our zero waste efforts are key.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We must overcome global resource constraints and ensure a safe and secure supply of critical resources, such as water, food and other materials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Closing resource loops and turning waste into resource will reduce our vulnerability to global supply shocks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: One way that this can be done is through urban mining.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: A research group from Tsinghua University in China has found that recovering resources like gold, copper and other metals from e-waste is 13 times cheaper than mining them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: In the process, we do not need to go back to nature to exploit and restore it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The World Economic Forum estimates that 50 million tonnes of e-waste, equivalent to 120,000 jumbo jets, are produced globally each year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Imagine the potential in urban mining where precious metals can be mined from e-waste, and energy from food waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Figuratively speaking, we can look at Semakau not as a landfill for trash but as a treasure island right in our very own backyard.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: For Singapore companies to continue to thrive in the future economy, they must adapt to the growing constraints on carbon and other resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Globally, a number of businesses are already taking the lead to adopt a more circular supply chain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This could entail using recycled materials as raw materials, extending the life of products or recovering resources from products at the end of life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Unilever has introduced post-consumer recycled waste materials into products, such as dishwashing liquid detergent bottles, with some of their brands using 100% recycled polyethylene terephthalate (PET) packaging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Similarly, automobile companies like General Motors and BMW are working with renewable-energy storage suppliers to create an aftermarket for end-of-life batteries for electric and hybrid vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These new business models will open new economic opportunities and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This includes indirect benefits, such as helping our companies export overseas and creating jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Singapore must adopt a circular economy approach to build these three resiliences and sustain future growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We must make every effort to close our resource loops and reuse our resources for as long as possible and this is not new to us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We have done so for water and, in fact, even for waste streams, such as construction and demolition waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This is the approach we must also take for other resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Resource Sustainability Bill will, for the first time, put in place a systems-level approach that mandates key responsibilities to enable reuse and recycling nationwide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will complement and support the voluntary efforts of our people and private sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Bill will bring our regulatory framework upstream.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: It will send economic signals to producers, such as manufacturers and importers, to take into account the cost of environmental externalities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: It also encourages innovation and the redesigning of products that require less materials, last longer and are more easily recycled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The regulatory framework will also fund the recovery and aggregation of useful materials, such as metals from e-waste, which makes recycling more viable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We will target the three priority waste streams of electrical and electronic waste, or e-waste, packaging waste, including plastics, and food waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: E-waste generation is growing exponentially with rising affluence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This translates to each person throwing away the equivalent of six mobile phones every month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Such waste may contain heavy metals and other hazardous substances, and improper disposal may lead to the contamination of our environment and harm public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will mandate producers of covered electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) to be responsible for the collection and proper treatment of their e-waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: All producers of covered EEE will need to register with the National Environment Agency (NEA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Producers of consumer products which exceed the prescribed thresholds will need to join the Producer Responsibility Scheme (PRS) and finance the collection and recycling of e-waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: In return, the PRS operator will be responsible for meeting e-waste collection targets set by NEA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: To minimise the regulatory impact on smaller players, we have set thresholds to exempt smaller producers, which supply about 10% of the consumer products that are put-to-market in Singapore by weight, from joining PRS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This means that producers of 90% of the consumer products put-to-market in Singapore will be subjected to the EPR framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We will monitor the implementation of the EPR framework and ensure that these thresholds remain relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The next priority waste stream is packaging waste, including plastics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We generate large amounts of this – around a third of the total domestic waste disposed of in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Almost all of this packaging material is incinerated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This ensures that the environmental impacts are managed effectively, and our packaging, including plastics, do not end up in the sea, mangling creatures, such as cute baby dugongs in Thailand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: However, we ought to do more to reduce and recycle packaging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: External forces are also changing the economics of the recycling industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: China’s ban on the import of plastic waste has shifted the trade patterns of plastic recyclables.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We can and must do more to better manage packaging, including plastics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: As a start, next year, we will implement mandatory reporting of packaging data as well as plans to reduce, reuse or recycle packaging, including plastics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The requirements will apply, for a start, to companies with an annual turnover of over $10 million.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will cover approximately 4,500 medium and large enterprises in Singapore which put packaging on the market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This reporting will focus management attention on the packaging that companies are placing on the market and spur reduction efforts that will save them costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will lay the ground for an EPR framework for packaging waste, which will be put in place no later than 2025, if not earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Third, food waste is a major waste stream with high generation tonnage and low recycling rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: In 2018, we generated 763,000 tonnes of food waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: In preparation for this, we will require developers of new buildings which are expected to be large food waste generators to make provisions for onsite treatment of food waste in development plans submitted from 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These new requirements will ensure that food waste from large food waste generators is diverted for treatment or converted into useful products, such as compost and animal feed, instead of being incinerated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will also reduce odour and pest nuisances at the premises, and reduce the contamination of recyclables by food waste, allowing for greater resource recovery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We will complement the regulatory frameworks with other measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These include educational campaigns, co-creation efforts with the community and grants to support ground-up initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: For example, NEA launched the "Say YES to Waste Less" campaign in June as part of the Year Towards Zero Waste movement to reduce the excessive consumption of disposables and packaging and encourage the use of reusables.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: NEA has also launched the "Towards Zero Waste Grant" to support individuals, interest groups, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), grassroots organisations and corporations to initiate or scale up waste reduction and recycling initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: A vibrant Zero Waste ecosystem will encourage our citizens to reduce, reuse and recycle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Our regulatory measures will be key in incentivising producers to play an active role in building this Zero Waste ecosystem with us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Part 3 of the Bill establishes the EPR framework for e-waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: For producers of regulated non-consumer products, clause 13 requires them to collect any of such products upon request by customers at no charge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 14 requires retailers to offer a one-for-one collection of an unwanted product at no charge when retailers deliver a product of the same type to a customer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 15 requires large retailers to provide in-store collection of e-waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Retailers are important stakeholders in this EPR framework for e-waste and are often the interface with customers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: To ensure that e-waste is properly managed and disposed of, clauses 16 and 17 lay out restrictions on the collection and disposal of e-waste to ensure proper treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The next part of the Bill, Part 4, establishes the mandatory reporting framework for packaging, including plastics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 20 requires producers of specified packaging that fulfil the threshold criteria to report on the packaging they introduce onto the Singapore market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: They will also be required to submit plans to NEA to reduce, reuse or recycle packaging under clause 21.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Part 5 establishes the mandatory segregation of food waste for treatment for buildings which are large generators of food waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 25 requires occupiers of a prescribed building to segregate their food waste and dispose of it in a facility provided by the building manager, who will be obligated to provide such facilities under clause 26.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 27 requires the building managers of prescribed buildings to also ensure the treatment of all food waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Part 6 covers the requirements on operators of the PRS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: They are fundamental in any EPR framework as they establish the network for public collection of the regulated waste and ensure that the waste collected is properly treated and recycled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 28 will require operators of the PRS to be licensed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clauses 30 to 32 empower NEA to determine the conditions of the licence and to take necessary actions to ensure effective operation of the PRS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: As NEA will be providing the licensee with certain information submitted by obligated producers for the purpose of the EPR, clause 36 makes it an offence for the licensee or former licensees to disclose any confidential information received from NEA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will ensure the confidentiality of data to safeguard the interests of producers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Part 7 contains the provisions necessary for the enforcement of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clauses 37 to 40 empower authorised officers to request for information and documents from any person and enter any non-residential premises to investigate or monitor compliance with the provisions of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 41 penalises anyone who hinders an authorised officer in the performance of his or her duty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Part 8 contains miscellaneous provisions necessary for the administration of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: As a large part of the regulations is dependent on information furnished by the obligated persons, clause 42 makes the provision of any false or misleading information an offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: To safeguard information, clause 43 prohibits NEA from disclosing any confidential information or document except in accordance with the clause.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The penalties laid out in the Bill are in line with other similar legislation, such as the Energy Conservation Act and the Environmental Public Health Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The impacts of climate change and the carbon and resource constraints we face respect no geographical or national boundaries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot afford to leave it to future generations to worry about.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad to hear that we are planning for both climate change and rising sea levels and doing our best to use resources sustainably.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is a worthwhile goal but a very big one.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We will all need to pull together to achieve it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I often hear Singaporeans say, "But we are such a small country, how can we make a difference?" Indeed, our carbon footprint is comparatively low compared to other larger countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But this effort can put us as a world leader on the international stage and, hopefully, we can inspire others to do their part.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If companies do not meet the targets, what penalties will be imposed?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need ambitious targets to ensure that companies take this seriously but, at the same time, it should not be too onerous.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Companies should not be unduly over-pressurised by this requirement.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After all, doing business nowadays is not easy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, the Government also needs to simplify reporting as much as possible and train companies accordingly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the new requirements raise the prices of goods?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some eateries, hawker centres and fast-food restaurants, for example, provide single-use plastic spoons and forks for customers having their meals onsite.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If not, that could become a loophole in the law.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, if the Minister can explain more on electrical and electronic waste.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Given the expected increase in volume of e-waste, can our current e-waste recycling capability cope?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are the plans to grow this capability?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It concerns me that building managers will have difficulties implementing segregation and treating of food waste onsite, especially if occupiers of the prescribed buildings do not cooperate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This would be just like our Housing and Development Board (HDB) recycling bins, where just one uncooperative person can contaminate the whole bin.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on how massive is this exercise?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How many buildings would fall within this category?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How many NEA-operated hawker centres have such facilities at the moment?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How would food prices at hawker centres, coffee shops, schools and so on be affected?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are there local commercial buildings that have already adopted the practice of segregating and/or treating food waste onsite?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are their challenges, the results and benefits?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But individual actions will make a difference, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What I hope to see is this message trickling down to individuals.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Nothing is too small or too little to combat climate change for our next generation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, I would like to take this opportunity to once again call for a charge on plastic bags.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The impact may be insignificant, as the Senior Minister of State alluded to in her reply to my Parliamentary Question recently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But I strongly believe that such a gesture will make people more conscious of what they do, how many plastic bags do they need and such consciousness will have knock-on effects on their daily lives and the consumption pattern.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, we must stop consuming more than what we need.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Reduce, reuse, recycle must be the norm of our society.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Fighting climate change should not be the job of just the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And we have to do this seriously for the survival of our country and for our next generation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we please do more to get all residents to use recycling bins appropriately?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are there plans to improve the heartland recycling network?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, many depend on the "karang guni" man to dispose of our unwanted items.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How will this new Bill impact their trade?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another facet of our life is the personal mobility devices (PMDs).

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How are people to dispose of their PMDs?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister give some guidance in these areas?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Domestic helpers and foreign workers play a big role at home and at work when it comes to waste management.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is the Ministry doing to reach out to these groups?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Everyone has a duty to protect the Earth.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill stipulates that large companies must inform authorities how much single-use packaging they are using and how to reduce packaging.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But at the same time, we must also be aware of price increases brought about by the new regulations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill also stipulates that food waste must be processed in a special machine.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How are they going to train tenants of a building?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We do not want it to be like our HDB recycling bins where just one person can contaminate the whole bin, causing all items inside to become unrecyclable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Separately, will the new regulations affect food prices?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Talking about recycling in the HDB precincts, how will the new regulations affect the karang guni or rag-and-bone men?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are many people who are about to change their PMDs to the ones that comply with the UL2272 standard.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Whether it is at commercial premises or at home, foreign workers and domestic helpers play a big role in waste management.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The amount of solid waste disposed of has increased exponentially due to our affluence, population growth and consumption habits.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a ticking time bomb that needs urgency in tackling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am, therefore, heartened to see efforts being dedicated towards that end.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Resource Sustainability Bill we have before us is a timely addition to Singapore's waste management strategy by targeting the three main streams of waste in Singapore: electrical or electronic products and e-waste, food waste and packaging, and I support the Bill's aims to augment our waste management strategies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I would like to touch on a few topics related to circularity and resource sustainability, and I hope the Minister can clarify on how they will be addressed moving forward.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There has been much coverage over the impact of packaging waste on our environment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, our reliance on such single-use packaging has only continued to deepen despite efforts, such as the voluntary Singapore Packaging Agreement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, this House has unsurprisingly seen much debate over single-use plastics, including those used for packaging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, data on the detailed use of such packaging does not seem to be tracked for now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, mandatory packaging reporting seems necessary as a first step towards a framework to regulate packaging products.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And such is the case under Part 4 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under clause 20 of the Bill, companies are required to submit a report relating to the specified packaging provided that they fulfil the prescribed threshold criteria.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a start, but I do have some concerns.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore currently serves as a key market and a regional showcase for many companies and franchisees, be it homegrown brands or foreign brands.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The packaging waste generated by many such companies can be substantial, including companies or businesses with not more than a turnover of $10 million.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State why a revenue threshold was chosen in the reporting standard?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The concern here is that by focusing on the bigger players, we may be losing sight of the small and medium enterprises (SMEs) or the smaller businesses which may be used to single-use plastics as they have no resources to work on alternatives.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will the Ministry help businesses below that turnover threshold limit their packaging, especially businesses that have always used much packaging, for example, food and other retail businesses?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This issue is important to get right, especially for currently small but fast-growing companies, such as Grain and Wok Hey.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Helping them with packaging standards at first will be more cost-effective than to have them switch over and comply with new standards at a later date.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, since producers of specified packaging who fulfil the prescribed threshold criteria in any year – let us call it "T" – must, in year T+2, submit to NEA a report relating to the specified packaging that is imported or used in year T+1, it appears that there will be a two-year time lag in calculating the total amount of packaging reported.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, the earliest this information will be reported will be in 2021, as noted in the news.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the meantime, how will NEA work to ensure that between now and 2021, the companies will actively work towards less packaging?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has there been any companies that have given information to the relevant agencies on this?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A clear benefit of releasing such data is to let relevant organisations use it for a Green Score system that allows companies to be judged on their efforts and targets to reduce packaging waste.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can incentivise companies to work towards reduction targets as an interim measure until NEA releases an EPR scheme for packaging companies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Key waste statistics from NEA indicate that while food waste stands at 10% of all waste generated, recycling stands at 17% of the food waste generated in 2018.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is an improvement from 6% in 2003 but, evidently, more can be done to tackle the remaining waste.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, our campaign against food waste seems lacklustre.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The year-long Food Waste campaign is non-binding on citizens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In many Government and university events, anecdotes of good catered food going to waste as they are left unconsumed are a dime a dozen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as we must balance the needs between hygiene and waste management, the fact remains that food waste is a fundamental issue that requires bigger changes, indeed, an overhaul, to ensure that the loop can be closed and allow for effective regeneration of such resources.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the news, there are reports of plans from the Public Utilities Board (PUB) to treat food waste into biogas at Tuas Nexus and of urban insect farms supported by Enterprise Singapore that are targeted at the food waste issue as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such grandiose plans, however, will take time to integrate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the meantime, perhaps making consumption adjustments on major waste producers will see more immediate impact.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As clause 4 of the Bill binds the Government on the provisions of the Bill, we could start from the Public Service to signal the seriousness that this Government takes in tackling a fundamental issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How would the Public Service support efforts to reduce food waste internally?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have seen in a Straits Times Forum reply that the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) tries to keep food waste to a minimum.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could be extended to the whole of the Public Service, with a firm public commitment to lead by example and reduce food waste that it produces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will send a good signal to the private sector and can even be a good way to reduce overheads in holding events, however slight.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, under the Bill, occupiers of a prescribed building or part of a prescribed building must segregate food waste.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to food waste segregation facilities, building managers of a new building must also provide treatment facilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, with the proliferation of digital devices, e-waste is increasingly a problem.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many households keep devices that no longer work, not knowing where to dispose of them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am, therefore, concerned about how certain provisions in the Bill may adversely hinder certain current e-waste collection efforts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would these provisions within this Bill negatively affect well-intended public collection?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How about the "karang guni" men who also provide collection services?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am of the view that NEA should encourage ground-up initiatives from members of the public, NGOs and small shops to enable such recycling in conjunction with industry stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, I hope that such written permission from NEA will be easy to obtain at little to no cost if they are doing such public collection with good intentions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask the Senior Minister of State how does the Ministry intend to enforce against retailers when they fall foul of the provisions of the Bill after it is passed and what recourse would the public have if retailers refuse to accept e-waste.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What recourse can the public take to effectively report errant behaviour on the part of such retailers?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was noted by the Senior Minister of State in the Committee of Supply (COS) debate in 2018 that through aggregating e-waste and enabling more efficient collection and processing, there would be greater value captured from e-waste and can help offset the cost of operating the e-waste management system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the small but burgeoning e-waste recycling industry will be boosted by the introduction of this framework, I hope some insights and assurances can be given on regulating precious metal recovery from e-waste.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, how do we ensure that the export of our e-waste for recycling purposes, such that the Basel Convention is compiled with, and that the e-waste does not end up in a black market overseas?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the potentially hazardous chemicals involved in recycling, what safety regulations are in place to ensure that such chemicals do not find themselves into the environment?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such news is disconcerting, as such waste exports have been a source of diplomatic tensions and we do not want to impact the environment of our neighbours adversely.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ministerial reassurances in this area will go some way to assuage concerns on the impact on our environment or that we may be exporting our e-waste problem away, to the detriment of our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Tackling the main streams of waste is key to minimising marine pollution that has impacted not just our shorelines, but also the shorelines and waterways of our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wish to add my voice to support the recent Bangkok Declaration on combating Marine Debris that Singapore has adopted, but I hope we can do more on the preventative end.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A key source of marine pollution has been micro plastics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore has not been immune from this source of pollution, with micro plastics in our own coastline found to be carrying toxic pathogens that cause coral bleaching and wound infections.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such bans have been introduced in the European Union (EU), to be enforced from 2020.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that banning the production of micro plastics will send a good signal in our commitment to reduce the impact of micro plastics on our environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When something is thrown away, it does not disappear; it has to be disposed of somewhere or somehow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After reducing the volume of unrecycled waste through burning which produces energy, we need to put the remaining ashes somewhere.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Landfills serve this purpose but, as the name connotes, it fills land and land is not something we have in abundance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to be good stewards of it; we cannot waste it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have already used up substantial areas in Choa Chu Kang, Lim Chu Kang and Lorong Halus as landfills.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Pulau Semakau is currently a key landfill and we cannot afford to waste it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the past 40 years, the amount of waste increased seven-fold, with food waste increasing 30% in the last 10 years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What we are aiming for is to prolong this for as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill supports the endeavour by addressing electrical and electronic waste, packaging waste and food waste.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Part 3 of this Bill addresses electrical and electronic waste.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It makes sure users have a way to recycle these products.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 13 requires producers of non-consumer products to collect upon request what was produced or manufactured.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 15 requires large retailers to accept used products similar to those they sell in order to dispose of them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 14 requires retailers who deliver products to accept and dispose of the old item.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would be especially useful for bulky electric products, such as washing machines and fridges.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not only would this reduce the toxicity of waste going to our landfill, it will also be able to extract valuable minerals and materials from these used products, finding treasure in the trash.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will reduce the demand on mining and make these limited resources on the earth last longer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In essence, we have a duty in Parliament to ensure we entrench a sustainable plan to protect our green environment, reduce plastic-usage, increase recycling, enhance upcycling.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If done correctly, Singapore can be a global thought leader on this.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It must be a united effort across all sectors of our society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Collection is the first step and there is a need to encourage and promote collection.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is done by requiring operators of the responsible producer scheme to hit a target collection in clause 30(c) and by requiring them to promote awareness of electronic waste disposal in clause 30(d).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After collection, the waste needs to be dealt with properly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 12 requires producers to manage electronic waste by becoming a member of a responsible producer scheme, which is regulated by Part 6 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as the consequences are quite serious for non-compliance, would the Minister explain how they will work with and assist those arrested and affected understand how to comply with this legislation?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, as this Bill addresses regulated products, would the Minister explain how this might affect e-commerce of electronic products and how are concerns that those required to accept or collect waste might become inequitably burdened by waste that they were not responsible for producing, that is, how are these concerns going to be addressed?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides electronic waste, another important source of waste that this Bill seeks to address is packaging waste.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Part 4 institutes a reporting regime relating to packaging which requires producers of specified packaging to monitor its packaging waste and to think about ways to reduce, reuse or recycle packaging.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These reports are to be submitted according to the years that the producers hit the prescribed limit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The flexibility in such a scheme is good.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It encourages producers to be aware of what they are producing, why they are producing it and how they can reduce it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, on the other hand, producers figure out for themselves how to get to the end goal of reducing packaging waste, allowing them to prioritise what they are looking for in packaging, accommodating the variety of purposes packaging may serve for that product.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, drink powder sachets apportion the powder, make it portable, differentiate sachet contents and protects it from getting wet.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, on the other hand, more environmentally-friendly packaging, such as paper-based packaging, may serve similar functions instead.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Relating to recycling packaging, I have three questions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If so, is it feasible to tweak our waste management system to better tap into the biodegradable ability of these biodegradable plastics?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, what plans are there to increase our capability to recycle our own waste product, especially plastic waste?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important since there are reports that recyclable waste is ending up incinerated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, because trash can be treasures for a different product, how can Singapore tap into upcycling our waste and promoting a circular economy even though Singapore may not have a very big manufacturing sector ourselves?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The third kind of waste this Bill addresses is in Part 5, being food waste.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If that building is an existing building, clause 27(2) allows the food waste management process to be outsourced instead of being situated onsite but the food must still be segregated and treated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although the building manager needs to provide such a facility, the duty is not left to the building's management alone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An occupier is compelled to make use of it through clause 25 which creates an offence for an occupier of such buildings to dispose of food waste together with other types of waste if the food waste was generated in that building.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because food was not left exposed overnight, pest and rodent problems are minimised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Food compost are used as fertilisers and non-potable water used for cleaning the eco-digester, rubbish bins or bin centres.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Ministry kindly elaborate on who are the intended prescribed buildings?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would they include shopping malls and hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides dealing with food waste through a food waste management system, there is a need to minimise food contaminating recyclable items.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Perhaps the Ministry could consider requiring regular dustbins be situated near recycling bins so that the inconsiderate actions of a few will not hamper the recycling efforts of the majority.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is being done to increase recycling literacy and how effective has it been?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, is the measure of unusability whether something is old and faded rather than spoilt and inoperable?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of reusing old mindsets, maybe we should discard them to have new ones – new ones that help us be content with what we have; new ones that help us prioritise responsible disposal over personal convenience; new ones that promote conscientious stewardship of our landfill over more short-sighted enjoyment of the temporal, without caring about the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to change the way we conceptualise, handle and create waste.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill provides the important infrastructural support for that change and, therefore, I support it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister addressed the Climate Emergency in his National Day Rally speech recently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even before this Climate Emergency, Singapore has been facing a Waste Emergency for decades now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We only have 15-odd years left to solve this problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We knew about this emergency for a while and yet our responses have not been as strong as they should be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In laying the framework to compel producers of e-waste, packaging waste and food waste to reduce, reuse and recycle their waste, this Bill is good, though late in coming.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a lot of discussion about the circular economy approach to addressing the problematic waste streams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Zero Waste Master Plan is supposed to express the circular economy aspiration, to eliminate waste and to continually reuse resources in the production-consumption cycle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this ambitious enough for the Waste Emergency we are facing?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much will this slow down the filling up of Pulau Semakau and extend its lifespan?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What happens when Semakau is filled up eventually?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not up the ante to halving the daily waste by 2030?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to these general questions, I would like to discuss three aspects that I think are being neglected by the framework to be instituted by this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is that the treatment of the three waste streams does not address the issue of transnational waste cycles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second is that the treatment of the food waste stream is too focused on the waste itself and neglects the upstream causes of food waste, including the way we eat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third is that our public education approach is still stuck in the communication campaign model and neglects the more effective model of targeting problem areas smartly by social nudging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With regard to e-waste, the current framework targets producers of electronic and electrical goods with retail presence here in Singapore and also retail companies selling these goods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is still based on the brick-and-mortar economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the trend is for consumers to order their electronic goods online.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And it is not uncommon for small to medium-sized goods to be shipped from overseas these days through micro-retailers utilising online platforms to connect with consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How would the EPR framework apply to these micro-retailers and overseas producers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How would the e-waste from these production-consumption streams be audited and factored into the EPR system?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are not trivial questions as we should expect online shopping and transnational delivery to increase in scope and scale as technologies improve and society evolves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Online shopping and transnational delivery mean more packaging would be used to ensure goods are not damaged by extended shipping.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current framework targets producers of packaging and packaged producers with annual turnover of more than $10 million.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What percentage of packaging waste do these producers account for?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does this cover the growing online shopping arms of these producers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How about the growing field of micro-retailers and overseas producers selling to local consumers through online platforms?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of these countries are closing their doors to waste import, while there have been cases of waste dumping and e-waste pollution hurting local communities that give a bad name to countries that export waste like Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can we ensure that our exported recyclable wastes are properly processed and recycled?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What happens if we are not able to export the waste for recycling, for example, plastics and packaging wastes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not just an accountability issue, but it is also about the integrity of the circular economy approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we are not ensuring waste materials get returned to the production-consumption cycle, but are simply trying to get rid of thrash to prevent Semakau from filling up, then we are not keeping to the true spirit of the circular economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A significant portion, 144,000 tonnes are lost when imported food lands in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why is this so and what can MEWR do to reduce this unnecessary wastage?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second issue is that we need to go upstream to tackle the food waste, from tackling wastage in the food supply chain to the way the nation eats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should deploy the circular economy approach here, too, in a whole-of-system manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I mentioned the significant amount of food lost in the importing food chain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One solution is to increase local production to supply food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To this end, the Government is targeting to increase local production to meet 30% of local nutritional needs by 2030.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Increasing local food production will create other problems of food lost and wasted during the production process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MEWR should, therefore, look at this area and encourage the reusing of food lost during the production process as animal feed or their recycling into compost for farming.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The large-scale processing of food waste will also reap benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that when the Tuas Nexus comes online in 2025, food waste and used water sludge will be co-digested to produce biogas for energy production.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does this mean the tradeoff is that we will not be benefiting from composting food waste instead?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the options for food waste treatment either co-digestion to produce biogas or composting to produce fertiliser?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, what are the calculations of MEWR in choosing co-digestion rather than composting, since the production of compost fertiliser could benefit local farming?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current Bill targets commercial and industrial premises that generate large amounts of food waste to undertake food waste segregation for treatment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Residents even requested for the pilot to be extended.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the success and the popularity of the pilot and the fact that we are facing a waste emergency, should we not be bold and extend this now to all HDB estates?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We import 90% of our food and yet we consume in abundance with very little awareness of our food security issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A lot of wastage is caused by near-expiry food being thrown away by both retailers and consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, we have a not insignificant group of Singaporeans facing household food insecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to encourage food donation to reduce food waste.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have spoken on this before, during the debate on the Singapore Food Agency Bill, that the Government is in a good position to develop a National Food Support System to channel excess food to fight household food insecurity in Singapore and feed hungry Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also legislate Good Samaritan laws to protect food donors and food distributors from criminal or civil liability for incidents arising from donated excess food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third issue is that we have hit a green ceiling on education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to change our model from communication campaigns to strong and smart nudging, using the social norms held by Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The response by MEWR is to change the labels on the blue bins and paint the recycling trucks blue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we would identify a social norm that is blocking efforts to encourage domestic recycling and raising green consciousness across Singapore society, it is the norm of convenience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Convenience has become the norm that need no explanation when it comes to demand for Government and municipal services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To reduce littering, we make throwing rubbish convenient by placing green rubbish bins all over the city.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To promote a hygienic environment, we make garbage disposal convenient by building rubbish chutes in each home or on each floor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Using the same reason or excuse, we refuse to consider banning or discouraging plastic bag usage, so that residents can conveniently bag their garbage to dispose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whenever a slight inconvenience is caused by maintenance or repair works, we apologise for it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why the blue recycling bin has hit a green ceiling, because the big bin conveniently placed at the foot of the block by the side of the road is a convenient bin to dump any rubbish indiscriminately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the larger systemic level, we conveniently incinerate our rubbish when we can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to change this mindset of convenience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A true circular economy cannot have convenience as the dominant norm guiding our behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is why I think the Government is mistaken in its reluctance to tackle single-use plastics as such, despite the strong public calls to do it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not a populist move with little systemic impact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, tackling single-use plastics will not have as much impact on reducing the waste streams filling up Semakau than the complex EPR systems being put in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it has tremendous educational value that will nudge Singaporeans to change their whole approach to consumption and disposal of waste.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, single-use plastic water bottles, instead of drinking from a cup that has to be filled and washed, one just has to open, drink and throw.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we tackle single-use plastics, we are not just tackling the plastic, we are challenging the idea of convenience and undermining its importance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not have to ban plastic bags to do this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Likewise, I remember the early days of our National Recycling Programme, when green translucent recycling bags were dropped at the doors of each household.
