speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On each bag, there were diagrams showing what items can be recycled and what cannot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The recycling bags were inconvenient, because it required residents to place items into the bag and bring it out to the lift lobby on a specified date every fortnight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was also inconvenient as a system, because workers needed to go to each floor to collect the bags and bring them down to the truck.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it gave those who would try to recycle purpose and a sense of achievement, and the green bags at home reminded everyone to recycle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The circular economy approach is the right one to adopt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, we need to double down on education and get all Singaporeans to reduce, reuse and recycle as their second nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should do this by moving away from communication campaigns to social nudging, especially to shake up the norm of convenience at the heart of our problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not just about Semakau filling up, but it is also about how we see ourselves as citizens of this Earth, whether we should seek our own selfish convenience or to choose to protect Earth for the sake of our children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This Masterplan has been eagerly anticipated by the community and was ceremoniously launched last Friday.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I think even the Ministry was eager to get this going that the Bill was referred to as the Act in the Masterplan on the website when I checked in after the launch.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill’s intent is to fortify the regulatory teeth needed to ensure sustainability in the consumption of resources, which our planet has a finite amount of.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, the Bill can and must do much more to reflect the urgency of the climate crisis which I would like to discuss.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity with the Bill to urge the Government to take a bold and different perspective in solving the food security challenge for our vulnerable groups as a critical climate change action.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The United Nations International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), had warned in October 2018 that we only have 12 years, or 11 years now, for global warming to be kept to a maximum of 1.5 degrees celsius in order to limit climate change catastrophe per the Paris Agreement which we are a party of.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Please allow me to propose further measures that must be implemented to signal the urgency.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, smart targets and goals.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Having companies simply report on their plans to reduce, reuse or recycle products in the Bill is insufficient.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Reporting obligations have no bite if it is not accompanied by waste production limits and recycling targets for producers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must set SMART goals that are Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant and Time-bound so the producers can plan and prepare accordingly.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the EU Packaging Directive 2018 sets out that by 2025, 65% by weight of all packaging must be recycled, with specific recycling targets for each material, such as 50% for plastic and 75% for paper and cardboard.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: By 2030, the target for recycled packaging is increased to 70%, including 55% for plastic and 85% of paper and cardboard.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such reduction targets can be achieved with ingenuity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In 2018, Unilever launched a 3-litre bottle for their Omo laundry detergent brand in Brazil, with a formula at six times the concentration of the original, so it can be diluted in people’s homes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This has reduced the volume of plastic used by 75%.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Companies must also inform customers about maintenance and repair services, environmental impacts and materials.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Retailers should also actively inform customers of sustainable products.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We can emulate the ambitious target setting and look to have companies report their progress on waste minimisation year-on-year via a measure of waste per unit of product output.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we must encourage public accountability and corporate stewardship by mandating these reports to be made public.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, the Singapore Exchange listing rules already have sustainability reporting guidelines but with no specific metrics prescribed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If we would like to see resource sustainability as a core part of doing business, it would seem sensible to stipulate the targets above as a standard reporting requirement for all listed companies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the Hong Kong Stock Exchange had a recent consultation on ESG reporting to (a) "require disclosure of significant climate-related issues" and (b) amend the "Environmental" key performance indicators to require disclosure of relevant targets.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Third, to escalate the adoption of a sustainability mindset and ensure affordability, we could incentivise producers and retailers with tax rebates, so that these obligations do not merely end in increased costs for reporting and collection, and the possibility of penalty, all of which will ultimately be passed on to the consumers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In China and Thailand, the EPR schemes introduced subjected companies producing non-biodegradable goods to taxes and offered tax credits as incentives for companies that used waste as raw materials.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's Earth Overshoot Day for 2019 was 12 April 2019.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This means that if the world consumed like us, we would be consuming three times as much resources as the earth can regenerate in a given year.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If we were to drive true resource sustainability, we not only have to compel producers to reduce packaging and have mandatory take-back programmes, but we also need electronics producers and retailers to be truly incentivised to extend product lifetimes, ensure maintenance and repair services availability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is an area where legislation is fast moving in the EU.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, in France, planned obsolescence of an electronic product is a criminal offence.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are also ongoing discussions in the EU that expected product lifetime be labelled.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Of the 763,000 tonnes of food loss a year, let us assume conservatively that half of them, or 382,000 tonnes, can be salvaged and redistributed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One meal, conservatively, uses one kg and, therefore, we will get about 382 million meals from the redistributable food loss.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I shared this in my speech during the debate on the Singapore Food Agency Bill as well.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I know this is a simple calculation, but I think we get the point.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Prime Minister Lee sounded a clarion call for Singapore to recognise the threat that climate change poses to us.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must never forget that, for most of the world, Singapore included, the most vulnerable amongst us will be hit hardest.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Climate change is already affecting rice production in the Mekong Delta.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As temperature rises change agricultural productivity and sea level rises, food availability will inevitably be affected.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For the 400,000 food-insecure people in Singapore, any price increase is detrimental.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: SG Food Rescue is a small group of individuals, and they have demonstrated that there is much in our food value chain that can be saved and redistributed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, they collect twice a week for a total of 2,500 kg of unsold fresh produce.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Five hundred to 700 kg of that goes to charities, namely, Free Food For All, Beyond Social Services and St Theresa's Home that feed the needy, while the rest is sent to a soup kitchen in Little India, Krishna's Kitchen.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The soup kitchen processes the vegetables and turns them into meals to feed the hungry, especially migrant workers in the Little India area.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: About 200 kg ends up with a community initiative in Marine Terrace – just down the road from where I live – and one of the six public community fridges, benefiting low-income residents.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And we can do even more, and we need to do so urgently and systemically.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We can shape food-loss-reducing behaviours by changing our food labelling policies and also enacting the Good Samaritan laws.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, "use by", "sell by", "expiry date" and "best before" all mean expiry date, according to the Singapore Food Agency.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Products are not allowed to be sold or distributed in Singapore past that date.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is, therefore, a huge source of food waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In many jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom, Hong Kong, Australia and New Zealand, "use by", "best before" and "sell by" mean that after the food reaches its "use by" date, the quality and flavour of the food is lowered, but it could still be edible.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Studies found that when a link between date labels, food waste and its environmental impacts is made, the willingness-to-pay for expired food increases, particularly for expired frozen or recently expired semi-perishable products.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Food that has gone past its "best before" date can be donated to charities so long as its within six months of the "best before" date.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am pleased to note that Singapore Food Agency is exploring Good Samaritan laws to ease business concerns over the donation of excess food.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I strongly advocate for the implementation of such laws which have been implemented in countries, such as Italy and the United States, and have encouraged food donations and reduced food waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As I mentioned before, incentives to help drive corporate behaviours cannot be overlooked.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We could consider extending the underused Business-IPC Partnership Scheme (BIPs) to include donation of edible food that would otherwise go to waste to charities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When supported by the Good Samaritan laws, this is especially compelling for many businesses I know, like Samsui Supplies and Services, through the Company of Good, a corporate giving initiative by the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We could be relieving our financially strapped households of a huge burden.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She has zero income and survives on $500 per month from her Social Service Office.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As a beneficiary of Free Food For All, a charity that receives and redistributes donated food, she saves a minimum of $100 per month.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Larger families are able to save much more.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We would also be freeing up scarce resources dedicated to our social safety net for other essential needs, such as healthcare.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Companies must be nudged out of their comfort zones into a greener and more innovative direction as we work towards building a circular economy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill, and the Zero Waste Masterplan, is a step in the right direction, but it is not enough, not with the fierce urgency of the climate crisis, and rightful ambition that we must have to be a leader in climate change mitigation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And more than that, sustainability is also a social parameter to secure a more inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As urgent as addressing the looming threats of climate change by reducing significant food loss is the need to solve the food insecurity problem of so many fellow Singaporeans by redistributing this food loss.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.55 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, our journey towards sustainability started in the 1960s, when our late Mr Lee Kuan Yew laid down the foundations for a clean and green Singapore, even before it was trendy to be green.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even as we grappled with a fledgling economy and uncertain times, we consciously moved towards cleaner sources of energy, dedicated our resources to cleaning up our major waterways, as well as growing our Garden City.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Sustainability is anchored in our ability to identify solutions that creatively minimise the tradeoffs we have to make and yet allow us to achieve longer-term goals in multiple domains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In Singapore, it is a commitment to balanced growth that benefits both the current and future generations, as well as a commitment to creating a high-quality living environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Often, such sustainability solutions require that we are able to see different seemingly disjointed parts of our economy and society function as part of an integrated, interconnected ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, changes to the law to better manage how Singapore handles waste and to help businesses that reduce and recycle electronic waste, packaging waste and food leftovers are a good first step.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore is particularly vulnerable to global disruptions caused by climate change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A change in weather patterns likely contributed to this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we cannot solve the Amazon problem, we can and still must play our part here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This aim is also in line with the Government’s international obligations and reflects our support for the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals which were adopted in 2015.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill could also positively impact workers in providing new avenues for job creation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, more jobs would be created in supply chain management; or specialist fields, for instance, innovation and engineering, in streamlining waste disposal, recycling processes and optimising packaging designs of products.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The next generation of our younger Singaporeans entering the workforce will also have very exciting opportunities to play an integral part in the national effort to mitigate the effects of climate change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement is currently working with the tripartite partners to support our workers and young Singaporeans by ensuring skills acquisition training for new entrants and existing workers in the Environmental Services field.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, we note that this Bill could also affect businesses negatively through changes to existing jobs and companies' processes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This could be especially challenging in today’s global economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This could potentially translate to cost-cutting measures felt by workers or consumers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the longer term, companies may have to restructure their internal processes to reduce costs and promote innovation and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, I would like to check with the Minister how will the Ministry support businesses and workers through these short-term and long-term changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Specifically, should there be extensions and/or staggering of timelines to encourage compliance by companies and time for workers to adapt?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Do we expect to provide time also for workers to take on the necessary training?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should aim to enable workers to keep their jobs while ensuring that this process continues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, we also cannot leave our SMEs behind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can more assistance be provided to the smaller ones which might struggle to afford the resources for compliance?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could grants be provided to smaller companies to help them comply?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement will support workers through this transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is prepared to work with the Ministry to help our workers and companies adapt to this change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have some technical points of clarification that I would like to seek from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, section 7(3) appears to exempt any manufacturer of regulated products from being considered as "producers" and, therefore, subject to registration and/or licensed scheme requirements, if the regulated product was manufactured “for or on behalf of” a "Singapore-connected person".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Section 19(2) is similar in the context of the use of "specified packaging".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would we know whether a manufacturer of a regulated product would specifically be manufacturing the product “for or on behalf of a Singapore-connected person”?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Are there estimates as to how many companies could feasibly take shelter under this exemption?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On the face of it, it appears that many products supplied and manufactured in Singapore would generally be manufactured for or on behalf of Singapore-connected persons, that is, Singapore Citizens/Permanent Residents or companies with a Singapore connection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, section 12(1)/(2) and section 20(1) make reference to the thresholds which the Minister may prescribe for regulated consumer products and packaging respectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can we have clarification on how the "prescribed threshold" will be determined?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the criteria and how will these be determined?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As mentioned by the Prime Minister in his National Day Rally speech, whilst we may not be able to halt climate change by ourselves, we all need to do our part to contribute to the global effort.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This has necessitated us to import resources in order for us to build up our infrastructure and built environment to allow for Singaporeans to live, work and play as they do today.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Likewise, 90% of our food is imported from outside of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is in addition to the natural gas and liquefied natural gas that we import to generate 95% of our electricity.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In other words, we are heavily reliant on supplies that we import to survive.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: There should be no illusions that we can survive in isolation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Yet, we are victims of our own success.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our economic growth has caused Singaporeans to become affluent and we have developed a tendency to overconsume.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This over-consumption is not isolated to merely food but also other resources, such as electrical and electronic appliances.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is inevitable that these will affect Singaporeans, given our need to import resources.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As such, all of us must play our part and make sustainability a way of life in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Bill provides a good first step in encouraging the responsible consumption of resources and the proper disposal of e-waste and food waste among Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is also a good starting point in the creation of a sustainable ecosystem to manage waste in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: With the proliferation of e-commerce, it is conceivable that e-retailers sell a comparable amount, if not more, in comparison to traditional brick-and-mortar retailers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: How does the Ministry intend for these retailers to provide these physical collection points when they do not have any physical stores?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, the stipulations of paragraphs 14 and 15 are likely to cause large retailers of electrical and electronic appliances to incur additional costs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Has the Ministry studied how it can help to offset some of these costs?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, the Government should consider providing grants or tax breaks.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These grants or tax breaks can be given when businesses invest in infrastructure to promote sustainable practices, such as the setting up of in-store collection points and waste recycling centres.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, the Government can look into the possibility of renting industrial buildings to these retailers at subsidised prices if they are used for waste disposal processes, such as consolidation or sorting.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can learn from the state government of Victoria, Australia, which provides grants and funding for programmes contributing to sustainability, including infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can learn from the Victorian government in incentivising the creation of waste disposal infrastructure in our nation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will not only help businesses in reducing costs associated with developing their own systems to monitor and track these products, but it will also help the Government in aggregating data on a national scale.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will help it to identify ways in which schemes can be improved upon, and programmes introduced, in order to ramp up sustainability efforts.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is not sufficient to simply assign the responsibility to businesses.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The contributions of businesses in efforts, such as carrying energy-efficient appliances, promoting the purchase of these, providing attractive trade-in deals to incentivise consumers to use energy-efficient products, and setting up more e-waste recycling points are bound to aid in sustainability.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the pursuit of sustainability should be a collective effort by Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are drawbacks to imposing the bulk of responsibility on the retailers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, this will result in rising business expenditures for the retailers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In turn, they will pass on these increased costs to consumers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This may disincentivise Singaporeans from procuring more energy-efficient appliances and keeping up with technological advancements.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The former will definitely not support environmentalism, while the latter will create speed bumps in our drive to make Singapore a smart nation and a global tech hub.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, the Government should launch an education campaign aimed at educating businesses and consumers on how to properly dispose of various kinds of waste, including food and e-waste.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The goal of this campaign is to ultimately ingrain sustainable practices into the subconscious of each and every Singaporean, in a similar fashion to how the proper separation of waste has become a given to most Japanese people.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, in relation to education pertaining to consumers and businesses, the Government should aim for the three following policy outcomes.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: One, for consumers and businesses to make every conscious effort to fight climate change and engage in sustainable practices, such as using energy-efficient appliances and purchasing the right amount of food.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Two, for responsible consumption and proper disposal of waste to become second nature to consumers and businesses.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Three, for consumers and businesses to encourage others to adhere to sustainable practices, through whistleblowing or otherwise, and to prevent the indiscriminate disposal of waste.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Low-income households are unable, rather than unwilling, to replace these.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It would be beneficial if the Government can provide tax breaks for these companies as their actions will help not just the environment, but also our less fortunate.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Struggling households will greatly benefit from receiving this food while we make strides in cutting down on waste.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe that the best solution to solving our issues pertaining to waste is to foster an environmentally-conscious society on all levels and across all sectors, in which the pursuit of reduced waste is a concept which is ingrained on a subconscious level in Singaporean businesses, people and the Government.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In the face of scorching temperatures, environmental degradation and climate change, the Resource Sustainability Bill, an entirely new Bill to address these critical issues, is very welcome, indeed.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We, in Singapore, have become well-acquainted with the 3Rs – reduce, reuse and recycle – perhaps to the point that they have become somewhat trite and lost valuable traction.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In truth, although many of us try hard to practise these 3Rs, it seems like broader structural factors and norms are working against our best efforts.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This environmentally-minded young woman meticulously details the steps she takes daily to reduce her use of disposables.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: On most days, she succeeds remarkably with her inspiring arsenal of reusable cups, containers and cutlery, and enjoys her takeaway food like the rest of us.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But one day in July this year, she recounted in a post her distressing experience at a bakery while waiting behind another customer.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: She said, "When he was done paying, I was almost going to cry.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: First, the 13 buns, each in one plastic bag of its own.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Then he wanted six buns in one bag and seven buns in another, and he wanted them double-bagged.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Then he asked the cashier to give him one large bag to put everything into.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In one bakery trip for 13 buns, there was a total of 18 – eighteen plastic bags – used in one single transaction." I share her distress when I witness such scenes in bakeries, hawker centres and supermarkets.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: It seems that, as consumers, we have become so precious that food items must be individually packed for fear that they come into contact with one another.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Heaven forbid that we allow our floss buns to defile our chocolate croissants!

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, I often find it difficult to advise service staff that I do not wish to have my breads individually packed and that I have no need for disposable cutlery.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Many look at me with annoyance, as if I have disrupted their well-established work processes.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The broader structural factors we all labour under are norms set in place by industries and consumer expectations which have been shaped as a result.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Companies are keen to win over customers and see offering individual packaging and free bags as good service.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Consumers are, in turn, trained to expect and demand such provisions and this vicious cycle perpetuates itself countless times every single day.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Over time, such norms and expectations result in mountains of trash and ingrain in our people wasteful habits that generate more rubbish than we can handle.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These harmful norms and expectations exist not only in the food and beverage (F&B) but in virtually every industry.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to propose an alternative set of 3Rs that can take environmental sustainability at institutional and individual levels to a higher plane.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The Resource Sustainability Act will be an excellent initiative with regard to reinvention.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, this will motivate them to invest more heavily in reinventing their products so that waste generation is minimised.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: On the specific issue of e-waste that the Bill seeks to address, technology companies have for too long practised planned obsolescence to boost consumer demand.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They design lifespans of products, such as smartphones and laptop computers, to be artificially short so that consumers are forced to ditch functional products and acquire new ones.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Some devices are also designed to be difficult to repair, or with replacement parts that are tightly controlled by the company, thereby making it challenging to extend their lifespans through replacing faulty parts.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Consumers find it far easier to buy a whole new device and junk the old one.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In contrast, consider the Dutch social enterprise Fairphone which produces smartphones with significantly less environmental impact.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Fairphones are designed to be easy to open, repair and upgrade.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: For example, Fairphone owners can unscrew their phones and replace the cameras, thereby enjoying the latest technology without having to buy an entirely new phone.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Examples, such as Fairphone, show us that resource sustainability is achievable through reinvention, especially if we introduce the right levers.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The next "R" we must act upon is to recalibrate.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: It is time we recalibrate people's expectations for what constitutes excellent service and warm hospitality.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: When did we transform into a society where events must involve goody bags, bottled water and an oversupply of catered food?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: How did our homes start to be filled with conference "swag" – stuff we all get – that we dump into landfills after engaging in Marie-Kondo-inspired spring cleaning?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Thankfully, these norms need not be cast in stone.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Collectively, we can forge fresh norms that help to advance resource sustainability.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Every industry can identify positive disruptions to enhance environmental sustainability.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Once we create new norms, we recalibrate consumer expectations and break the cycle of wasteful product practices that seem to be more entrenched as we become more affluent.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond punitive measures that clearly have their place in our ecosystem, we must also consider introducing more schemes to reward companies and consumers for their efforts towards resource sustainability.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to introduce more incentive schemes for companies to invest in technology to extend the shelf life of food items.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We also have to encourage different players within the food supply chain to collaborate on practicable solutions to stemming food waste.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We should also develop Singapore as a centre where we specialise in innovations to transform food waste streams into valuable by-products.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: By rewarding such investments, collaborations and innovations, we can steer companies towards greater resource sustainability.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Step by step, through actions big and small, we can shift mindsets and change behaviour for the better.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I rise in support of the Resource Sustainability Bill.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Over the last few years, as sustainability took on greater prominence worldwide, I am happy to report that, as a federation, the Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF) has, through our various industry groups, held numerous events and dialogues with the manufacturing community with a focus on the journey towards Zero Waste.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, SMF has a function committee set up to advocate good practices specifically in the fields of health, safety, security and environment.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: One of the cross-industry collaborative examples which I am proud to share is that, for the first time, the packaging industry group and the F&B industry group jointly held the annual Packaging Council of Singapore Conference, titled "Journey towards Zero Waste".

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, while trade associations and chambers (TACs), such as SMF, continue to champion the need for environmental awareness and conservation, it is clear that there are some speed bumps which we must address preliminarily.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: These take the form of the following: business priorities and increasing costs; support for the required reporting processes; and thirdly, education, outreach and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This move brings Singapore on par with numerous similar collection and recycling initiatives worldwide, including Japan's Home Appliance Recycling Law, the EU's Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Directive (WEEE Directive), the US state recycling laws on waste electrical and electronic equipment.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Many multinational corporations have taken it upon themselves to include waste management into their business strategy as part of their sustainability responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I agree that more can be done and more companies in Singapore need to take active measures to be on par with global standards.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: There are already a number of retailer-driven collection initiatives in place in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With the collection efforts being moved to the producers as well, there is optimism that we will truly be able to close the loop and have some materials recovered for future use by the producers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, Mr Deputy Speaker, there is a legitimate and common concern for the industry – will there be any form of support, in terms of funding or subsidies, for the extra manpower or training of manpower for the required reporting processes detailed in this Bill?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I now move to speak on Packaging Waste.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The Packaging Council of Singapore (PCS) is an Industry Group of SMF representing the local packaging industry, not just locally but also at the world and Asian levels of the packaging world.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Since five years ago, PCS has been organising an Annual Star Awards to recognise outstanding packaging innovations, some of which have also won international acclaim.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: At this year’s awards held last month in August, Senior Minister of State for Health and Law Mr Edwin Tong graced the event as the Guest of Honour.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In his keynote speech at the event, Mr Edwin Tong noted that many of this year’s winners displayed environmental awareness by innovating packaging materials and design with the use of recycled or more environmentally friendly products.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While there is still much room to improve in this particular industry, especially in relation to packaging materials for the F&B industry, I am heartened to see companies already creating packaging solutions for commercial use by utilising recycled materials, such as crop waste and mineral stone, instead of plastics.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I am especially happy and proud to add that, of the 29 awardees of the awards this year, 20 were awarded to students from our local polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This demonstrates that our young and our future are already gearing up for a future where sustainable materials should take centrestage.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The next steps for the packaging industry would be for companies downstream to adopt and use sustainable solutions and thereby further encouraging future innovations.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, the use of such sustainable packaging may in some industries lead to increased costs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For some companies, and even some sole proprietors, such as those operating food stalls, the increase in such costs is not justifiable even if, indeed, in the long run, such options may prove to be more beneficial.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Minister if there are plans to incentivise the use of more sustainable packaging materials or disincentivise the use of non-environmentally friendly packaging.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, under this Bill, producers now have to report the amount of packaging put to market annually.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While this will definitely give an idea of the packaging volume we are dealing with, packaging producers share the same concerns as their electronic and electrical counterparts in terms of support required for the additional manpower which I stated earlier in my speech.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   The next area of focus of the Bill is that of food waste.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: When food is wasted, there is a need to source for more food to meet demand, which results in increased costs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Resources that were used to grow and deliver the food are also wasted and more resources are also consumed to dispose of the waste.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In the Journey to Zero Waste, businesses play a major role.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Adoption of smart storage and preparation processes reduces excess food production and wastage.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is undeniable that for food manufacturers, waste reduction and management are key, and this should be part of the long-term business operations for major companies.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: SMF is committed to continue to hold dialogues to assist companies on this journey.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For food producers seeking to treat their own food waste, they do see that this is a way forward.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, the concern from local companies operating at scale is what resources will be made available in terms of equipment and training since waste treatment is quite a specific process.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the generation of waste from the food industry can also be attributed to the transportation process of the supply chain.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: And relatedly, if more incentives can be made available for food manufacturers to buy more local farm produce?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For some businesses, especially SMEs, the actual or perceived costs of changing their business model towards a more sustainability-friendly model may, indeed, become the obstacle.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, may I ask the Minister if there are plans for the Ministry to help encourage financial institutions to give more "green financing" in the manufacturing sector?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While the "green financing" concept is relatively known to the building sector, this does not seem to have gained traction in other sectors.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Further, the manufacturing industry would like to lobby for more support for SMEs to help secure loans when they raise their sustainability standards.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This would also play a part in enabling the circular economy, as expressed by the Ministry for the electronics and food manufacturing industries.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, this Bill is welcomed because of the common consensus that this world does not belong to any one generation but always to the next.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the concerns that I have raised above are, indeed, legitimate concerns, especially in the current uncertain global economic climate.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As a strong advocate of Singapore's own brand of tripartite partnership of the Government, employers and employees working as one, I am confident that the issues I have raised earlier in my speech can be overcome.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Continued dialogue and cross-engagement amongst all three groups will be key.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The Government looks to the employers for their support in achieving the objectives of a sustainable future.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The employers look to the Government for direction and support, and the employees look to their employers to learn how their own individual conduct in the office can affect the environment.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The concerns, views and contributions of each individual group of the tripartite partnership must always be valued and should never be trivialised.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As a trade association, SMF has already been working closely with SEC on a couple of initiatives.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The first is to help industries embed green culture and DNA by certifying them with the "Eco-Office" mark which helps employees in companies better understand the co-relation between climate change and their behavioural attitudes in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The Eco-Manufacturing initiative will encourage companies to continue to set higher standards in sustainability.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I applaud the move to work with retailers and suppliers to collect and dispose of unwanted consumer and non-consumer products.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, my concern is whether the process of collecting and disposal of such items is affordable for businesses and consumers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry review processes and facilitate cooperation among stakeholders to take advantage of economies of scale to minimise duplication of routes, maximise storage efficiency and so forth?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, the expected high prices on goods are not quite fair to consumers who are not disposing of any items.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In order to ensure that recovery costs remain at an affordable level for businesses and consumers, can the authorities assist all parties to cooperate fully to reduce costs?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Customers who do not need recycling should not pay a higher fee.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Next, I would like to express my concern about the collection processes in place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If they are not, I would like to suggest that stakeholders be provided guidance and infrastructural and administrative support from the various Government departments involved.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another concern is manpower and resource constraints, especially now that we have tightened up on the number of foreign workers allowed here.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a challenge, particularly for our SMEs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To make up for the shortfall in manpower, can more of our workers be trained to take on these tasks?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With these, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is a positive step in the right direction, and I wholeheartedly support it and I thank the Ministry for the Environment and Water Resources (MEWR) for taking this progressive step forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments proposed are substantive and will help to tackle the supply side of the equation and tackle it at the root rather than tackle the symptoms of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are starting the EPR framework with e-waste and, subsequently, packaging waste, and I hope we will soon extend it to other waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are all aware that when it comes to the environment, it cannot be business as usual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot go on generating and incinerating waste indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our landfills are rapidly filling up, and our planet is at her breaking point.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need become a zero-waste nation and we need to do it soon.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to remember that ensuring resource sustainability is not merely about waste management.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our efforts must both aim to manage waste and reduce the generation of waste in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our measures have to address both the producers on the supply side and the consumers on the demand side.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With this in mind, I would like to raise some clarifications and recommendations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a staggering loss of recoverable raw materials and a huge waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the envisaged collection targets in Singapore as a result of this Bill over the next three years?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What will be the next targets thereafter in the next three-year cycle?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how the collection targets are calculated?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also shed light on why is there a three-year grace period for missed collection targets?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this does not take into account e-commerce retailers, like other Members of this House have just raised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the rise of e-commerce, "large retailers" may not need to supply refuse collection points (RCPs) from a large shopfront area.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, all a "large retailer" needs is a warehouse and an Internet connection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister consider also requiring e-commerce retailers to partner with PRS operators or e-waste recyclers to collect and process unwanted e-products?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I understand that the Bill seeks to cover 90% of Singapore's e-waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, small producers will be exempted from financing critical producer responsibility schemes (PRS).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In line with the polluter-pays principle, PRS should not have the effect of excluding niche and low-volume producers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What measures will be imposed upon such small producers in the future in order that they be accountable for the e-waste that they generate?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As an interim measure, could the Ministry look into setting up subsidised, voluntary PRS schemes for such small producers who wish to contribute?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, I understand that producers with an annual turnover below $10 million will not need to report the packaging they imported or used and also need not submit to NEA a plan to reduce, reuse or recycle the packaging in Singapore, and how they will implement this plan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the $10 million threshold was determined and what proportion of the market these exempted producers of packaging waste form?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Small producers of low-cost goods can generate just as much waste as one with a high turnover.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister further share what plans there are to integrate these small producers into reporting schemes in the future?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I understand that a producer will submit their plan to reduce, reuse or recycle packaging and their implementation plans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I ask if there will be any penalties if these plans are not adhered to?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, in future, will MEWR consider setting reduction targets for these producers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, while we collect data from this exercise of submitting their plans, I am not sure we will achieve much in terms of reducing the amount of waste generated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to the broad framework under the Bill, we should also have initiatives on the ground to tackle the packaging waste generated by supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am astounded by the amount of unnecessary packaging used at supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While it is often argued that plastic is required to protect fresh produce during shipping and storage, I have been told that some items do not arrive already packaged in the plastic packaging that we see on the shelf.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are shipped in plastic packages and are then repackaged into even more plastic packaging.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I suggest we learn from what other countries have done to tackle waste generated at supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Major supermarket chains in the United Kingdom (UK), such as Waitrose and Morrisons, have gone "nude" by having "nude zones" where products are not packaged in plastic packaging.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would love to one day walk down our supermarkets in Singapore and see "nude" vegetables and fruits without any plastic packaging.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MEWR will consider launching a pilot for this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the supply side of the equation, we are doing well for e-waste and packaging waste where we are addressing the root of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, for food waste, we seem to be addressing the symptoms of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The focus of the Bill here is on processing the food waste rather than preventing or at least reducing it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We currently have technology on the market to identify and track the components of food waste for commercial businesses in order for them to plan their production better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One local example is the Singapore startup Good for Food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their Smart Dustbin allows hotels and large commercial kitchens to measure, track and identify all food waste thrown into it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The data allows businesses to adjust the type and quantity of food produced.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This prevents food waste and reduces business costs wasted on producing unsold and unconsumed food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We all know that if there is demand, there will always be supply.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Producers will likely continue to provide packaging and the EPR will simply be another business cost.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MEWR share what plans it has to urge Singaporeans to reduce and reuse?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know we have a lot of plans for recycling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I stress again that recycling does not address our throwaway culture.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to urge people to reduce and reuse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, a good economy will be useless for all of us if we do not have a healthy planet to live in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the words of Mdm Ho Ching, "There is no Plan B...because there is no Planet B." Notwithstanding the above queries, I stand in strong support of this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If you exclude the recycling of water, the first time Parliament debated the merits of recycling was in the 1983 Budget debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Member Mr Eric Cheong Yuen Chee suggested that the Economic Development Board set up industries to recycle industrial waste.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Recycling was quiescent for some years after, but it has been resurrected of late.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources must feel that recycling has been debated at nearly every other Sitting in the last few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We were a nation of conscientious recyclers until recently?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Or have we been shocked from our wasteful slumber?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is, like some fat around the middle, a bit of a sign that times are very good for most Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And like excess fat, trimming it will do us some good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I submit that recycling was hardly discussed from Independence through the 1980s because we were not rich yet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Recycling is both the necessity of the poor and the luxury of the rich.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It was obvious to the post-Independence Singaporean that our appliances – our television sets, radios, fridges and stoves – had to be repaired, refurbished, reused for as long as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It was obvious that letting food spoil today meant less food on the table tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Within our lifetime, many of us remember a vibrant, privately organised recycling industry for many of the wastes targeted by this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The karang guni men had a good trade in fixing and recycling scrap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Even food waste was collected for use by the pig farmers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, why did that grassroots recycling system break down?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The value of scrap materials is low and the costs of new manufacture are also low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, the cost of labour required to repair, refurbish or repurpose waste has increased significantly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Members will remember when soft drinks were sold in glass bottles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: When you finished your drink, the glass bottle would be collected and it would be washed and refilled at the factory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This practice has ceased because the costs of refilling have become too high, compared to the cost of providing single-use plastic or glass bottles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The goods that we consume – from consumer appliances to bottled drinks to food – they have no price attached to reflect the problems that their disposal will create.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Even in countries where bottle deposits and other taxes are applied to encourage recycling, the prices appear to be incorrect and too low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We know this because the world’s recycling infrastructure has essentially collapsed in just a few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As the Economist pointed out in an article on 15 June 2019, and I quote: "There is no point collecting recyclable waste unless someone is willing to buy it and actually do the recycling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Until late 2017, China was the world’s biggest importer of scrap by far.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The recycling trade is ironically unsustainable, premised on the assumption that the cost of recycling in developing countries would remain artificially low forever.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But these countries no longer wish to accept the world’s trash.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, what is heartening about this Bill and the Masterplan is that it confronts these economic realities squarely for the most part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It does not depend on the illusion of cheap recycling in some faraway land.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It recognises that real costs will be required to improve sustainability in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, I wish to discuss the three areas of focus in the Bill – electrical and electronic equipment waste, packaging and food waste.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) producers simply have little incentive to consider seriously how their products will be disposed of at end of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is efficient that they should bear responsibility for managing the lifecycle costs of their products.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My only concern here is how the regulatory cost will affect competition in this sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many retailers now operate largely or exclusively online.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While many brands only have a few authorised retailers in Singapore, parallel imports are common.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should ensure that regulation preserves competition as far as possible, while ensuring that retailers live up to their responsibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The question is how the EPR Framework can be customised for the needs and business models of the different stakeholders in the EEE retail space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, large EEE retailers are the focus of regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They will be expected to facilitate the disposal of e-waste for any products they supply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because collection of e-waste is not, and should not, be tied to new sales, large retailers are essentially providing a public service by using their scarce retail space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If all retailers were large, this would not distort competition, because all would be facing the same burden.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But smaller retailers and online retailers appear that they will escape this particular responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How then can we ensure that all retailers face the same regulatory costs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While the administrative burden may at first seem significant, especially for smaller retailers, the economics of scale of market platforms today means that a high proportion of EEE products are actually retailed or sold through only one of a few websites.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand there may be reluctance to impose new Government fees, the EPR will, in any case, result in costs for retailers, which will be passed on to consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is more important is that competition is preserved for consumers as this could more than offset any increases in cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I see the problem of excess packaging, at least for consumer goods, as essentially a coordination failure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Retailers would prefer to use less packaging but, because, we often believe attractive packaging is a sign of a product's quality, we encourage retailers to compete on how elaborate their packaging is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we have to be cautious about the tools we use to enforce this framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While I am not one to shy away from taxes when necessary, we have to avoid what the economist Prof Ng Yew Kwang calls the diamond goods effect: in a world with substantial packaging taxes, an over-packaged product is likely to be an excellent signal of the purchaser's wealth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One can hardly find the more luxurious mooncakes sold in plain boxes anymore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It appears that showing you can afford an expensive mooncake is far more important than how that mooncake actually tastes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To guard against making packaging appear even more valuable, perhaps we should consider creating limits on the amount of packaging that can be used.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This would encourage firms to compete on value, taste and price instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We are accustomed now to seeing food stalls, restaurants and hotels throwing out massive amounts of uneaten food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill will provide for the proper disposal of such food waste.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But obviously, we must also focus efforts on reducing the volume of food waste in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It may seem like a mystery why food retailers have so much wasted food, given that they lose money on unsold food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem seems to lie in how we, as consumers, make choices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Who among us likes to pick the last piece of fish at the economy rice stall?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How do we feel if we attend an event and the buffet runs out?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think it will be difficult to change our beliefs about food abundance and quality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We basically like to see an abundance of food as a signal of quality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we can encourage retailers to use technology and analytics to better plan how to serve their customers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Rayner Loi, a student at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, is running a startup, Good For Food, that uses AI-enabled dustbins to automatically identify and log the type of food waste disposed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think we need to recognise the central role of prices and regulation in setting our behaviour on a more sustainable path.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I agree there are some cultural practices that resist economic explanation, that harm sustainability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, our preference for meat products instead of vegetable or insect protein, that is a leading factor in unsustainable consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Impossible Foods and Beyond Burger, which market meat-free burger patties that taste like beef made headlines in Singapore and throughout the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I found this incredible, because Chinese vegetarians have been producing all manner of mock meats for centuries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is nothing new there, but clever marketing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is potential, therefore, to change our food culture, but I daresay the Government will not want to be the one to tell us to order "Mee Siam, mai (or minus) cockroach".

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, it is best to leave that to the private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is also much interest in behavioural interventions to promote recycling and more consideration for the environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Consumer recycling, for example, seems to be strongly driven by social norms, since recycling rates vary widely across the world, even in the absence of strong local regulations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The planned improvements in recycling signs for our blue bins will no doubt enhance recycling rates by providing more salient information to households on how to recycle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Social norm interventions, where people are told how their consumption patterns compare with those of their neighbours, have also been shown to generate sustained reductions in energy usage in large-scale randomised trials.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we should resist the temptation to believe that education and behavioural interventions alone can generate sustained change in consumption habits or eliminate a "throwaway culture".

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should not believe that sustainability branding can overcome basic economics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At some point this year, I think every organisation gave out a reusable bag or a reusable bottle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem, of course, is that this is inefficient if we do not reuse such bags or bottles often enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, let us replace branding exercises with hard policy decisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We would benefit tremendously from increasing their numbers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To try to make amends I bought solar power, which is more expensive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I have tried to eat less meat but I cannot bring myself to eat insects just yet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am only human but I am trying to be better.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Prime Minister highlighted the importance of climate change during the National Day Rally.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, there is enough evidence to suggest that the threat is bigger and sooner than 50 to 100 years away.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Climate science is imperfect in its predictions but all their errors have been to consistently underestimate the negative impact.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If anything, we should be moving even faster to prepare for a warmer and more variable climate.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Climate change is a complex issue with many facets.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For Singapore, we may think that as a small nation, what we do would not really have an impact on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But that is not to say that we can afford to ignore the consequences of our own actions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need to do the right thing so that we can have the moral authority to voice out in international fora for bigger nations to also do their part to fight climate change.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The first issue I wish to touch on is e-waste.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But even for the 20% that is supposedly recycled, they are not actually recycled but shipped overseas to be treated instead.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a hypocrisy that many governments will not admit to because they are busy winning the green voters.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But this comes at an enormous environmental cost to the importing countries and to their populations.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The policy bans various types of plastic, paper and solid waste from being exported to China.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It sent shock waves through the global recyclables market.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Waste started piling up in exporting countries, even in parking lots.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The changes resulted in waste being diverted to Southeast Asian countries, whose ports and facilities were ill-prepared to receive them in such high volume.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a result, Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia begun to enact their own restrictions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, the National Sword has several important implications for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To the extent that we are unable to recycle our own waste and rely on exports, this creates a bottleneck in the system.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Minister assure us that Singapore has the necessary facilities to treat e-waste and will not be exporting our problems to the rest of the world?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A second risk is pollution incidents resulting from the increased volume of waste being treated, particularly in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Minister also assure us that a pollution incident in Johor will not easily threaten our water supply?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Reducing packaging waste should be a win-win for all.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a consumer, I am often amazed by the almost comical amount of packaging that can surround one small device.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One computer mouse or one thumbdrive can be surrounded by packaging four to five times its size.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We see increasing reports of fish or whales that are dying because their stomachs are full of plastics.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Reducing waste would help producers save money while also saving the earth.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, while it is great that there is a requirement for producers of waste to submit plans to reduce, recycle or reuse the waste that they generate, I hope that the Minister can go further by prescribing a hard limit on the amount of waste to be reduced.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We do not seem to mandate reductions in the amount of packaging waste per dollar of product.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Should we be doing more to move the needle and aggressively drive down the amount of packaging waste produced?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, when the United States (US) introduced fuel efficiency targets for US carmarkers, they pushed for an aggressive improvement.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They wanted to go from around 30 miles per gallon in 2011 to 54.5 miles per gallon by 2025.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the Minister consider mandatory waste reduction guidelines?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is another area that is causing a big concern.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: According to the UN Food and Agricultural Organization, around 30% of the world's food production is lost or wasted annually.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from the economic and human cost, this has massive environmental impact as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
