text: In this Bill, the focus is on building managers to provide separate food waste disposal, to treat the food waste or send it to a licensed waste disposal facility.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would it be cheaper and more effective for the Government to provide this service in bulk through a regulated service provider and charge for this service?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If this is instead done piecemeal privately, is there a risk of higher costs?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even worse, would we be creating a bigger carbon footprint if transport is not efficient?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Overall, I laud this Bill as a good first step as it makes it easier to extract usable bioresources from our waste, which can then be used to produce biogas or electricity.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the same question applies here: can we not do more to reduce waste?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are we merely arranging deckchairs on the Titanic, while accelerating towards an iceberg?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yes, as a small country, our total waste is relatively small compared to the global total.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need to ask if we can do more to help the rest of the world reduce or deal with waste.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Technology and innovation are two assets that Singapore can leverage.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I remember past stories of companies being lauded for launching sustainable businesses, such as local food waste recycler IUT Global.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, many faded and shut down after a few years.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can we nurture national champions with deep expertise in managing waste in a commercially viable manner?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a nation, this is also an opportunity for us to take the lead on the international stage.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While climate change might be a divisive issue in some countries, or still seem distant to some people, waste is a more direct and tangible issue.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That should make it easier to rally people to take action.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Fighting global warming and environmental destruction is humanity's greatest test and, as the custodians of the earth, our greatest responsibility.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Sad to say, mankind has yet to pass this test or to rise up to our responsibility.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened by Singapore's affirmation of the Paris Accord.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am even prouder to know that when Singapore signs up for international agreements, including the Paris Accord, we have every intention and ability to abide by our commitments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Like many other things, unfortunately, Singapore is a price taker in the larger world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With our small carbon footprint, even if we cut emission to zero, the train on global warming has already left.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, we have to do our right and fair share, even if it does not tip the global scale, because we are a part of humanity and we share humanity's burden.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, fighting global warming and resource depletion is a grueling marathon, one that will test the resolve of successive generations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are real tradeoffs impacting real lives today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we must be practical in implementing it, focus on the most impactful ones, instead of the most fashionable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, there is much discussion about banning plastic bags or straws, despite Singapore's unique ability to deal with the negative impact.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: On the other hand, there are many other issues which are even more critical.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, one of the largest uses of global energy is for heating and air-conditioning.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And investing in better insulation and airflow design is not just impactful in reducing emissions, but it even pays off financially, factoring in the investment cost.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In financial terms, it is Net Present Value positive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And even better if Singaporeans can think about how to minimise the use of air-conditioning.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope more ground-up support, especially from the public, can be focused on these most impactful ideas to save our environment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our efforts must be rooted in facts, impact and practicality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we overreach, we risk undermining public support from the broader population across successive generations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And it is in this spirit that I would like to share feedback from the ground on how we can judiciously implement the good ideas that we have in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, the call to recycle large electrical and electronics equipment is a good move.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These may not be a very large source of waste, but they contain very toxic components.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I agree with the Government's effort to focus on larger sellers, get service providers to provide recycling service and to provide our businesses with sufficient time to adapt.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because it is not fair to put all the burden on the retail sellers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, we must give careful thought on how we implement this or we will see a noticeable increase in cost of living or reduce consumer choice.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One way to ensure careful implementation is to get the inputs from international environmental experts as well as major packaging companies, retailers and logistics players on what is practical and what can be reasonably done because sometimes there are real tradeoffs involved.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, many fresh products that we see in Singapore from Malaysia are prepacked into smaller packs prior to them being sent to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, if we take the view that we should reduce packaging and discourage smaller packs from being imported, then we have to do the bulk-breaking in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And given our high cost of labour, it will mean higher cost, which the consumers will end up paying for.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Also, for some brands that sell well in Singapore, there is ample scope for us to work with them to reduce packaging.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But for smaller brands, it may not be practical for Singapore to ask them to change the packaging just for Singapore because if we insist on doing that, we may end up reducing consumers' choices.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, we have to strike that balance there.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While I agree that many consumer products are over-packaged, we have to understand that companies have a natural desire to compete and differentiate, and that brings me to my final point about packaging which is that when consumers speak with their wallets, businesses have no choice but to listen.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fighting packaging waste, one of the strongest possible ways for us to strike the right balance is for the Government to support and, if necessary, fund consumer ground-up efforts to change consumer preferences for simple but effective packaging.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As a nation, we waste a tremendous amount of food.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I recently met with the voluntary welfare organisation, Food from the Heart.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Through a fantastic logistics network driven by dedicated staff and volunteers, they do outstanding work to bring food to people in need, food that would otherwise be wasted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They have recently decided to do substantial collaboration with Kebun Baru to help our needy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And I think that, as a nation, our effort to reduce food waste will benefit a lot if we consult food-based organisations, like Food from the Heart.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, if the Government can take the lead to work with other international organisations to help break down the environmental impact, perhaps by materials or the manufacturing process, this will help inform our passionate citizens who can then make a case to the rest of Singaporeans on the importance of moving away from fast fashion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When I visit regions and countries like Japan and Northern Europe, I realise that they are very conscious of the negative impact of fast fashion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that, on this issue, with some sufficient hard work down the road, we can encourage Singaporeans to buy in and be more thoughtful.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And if we succeed in doing so in Singapore, we will not just live up to our duty as part of humanity, but also, over time, what we do in this small part of the world can also influence and inspire similar acts beyond Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I declare my interest as a Director to National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) Foodfare and Advisor to Singapore Food Manufacturers' Association.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Just a decade ago, Pulau Semakau was expected to last until 2045.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But we have been producing so much waste over the last decade that we have shortened the lifespan of the landfill by another decade.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This trend is alarming and a cause for concern.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Designating 2019 as Singapore's year towards zero waste is a first step.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We have to do more in a more comprehensive, realistic and sustainable manner.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, this Bill aims to be comprehensive as it encompasses plans to deal with food, electronic and packaging waste.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I will focus on food waste in this speech.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In 2017, the National Environment Agency (NEA) launched the two-year "Love Your Food @ Schools Project" where some schools, including Chongzheng Primary in Tampines, are fitted with machines that guzzle food waste and turn them into compost and then given to residents who manage various community gardens.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: At Our Tampines Hub, we have two food waste digesters where up to 1.4 tonnes of food waste generated from the hawker centre can be recycled everyday into non-potable water and fertilizer which are also put to good use in our rooftop garden.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Over at the Singapore Armed Forces, food waste from some camps is being collected and treated to help generate energy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) and Westcom Solutions have a food digester in JTC's Pandan Loop Industrial Estate.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It processes food waste into an odourless organic fertiliser and produces about a ton of fertiliser every month which they packaged and sold.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: All these show that NEA has worked hard on food recycling seriously over the last few years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on what can this food waste be turned into other than fertilisers, energy and animal feed?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Is there a market for these products to be exported and sold?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Do we have the technology and capacity to do this?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How are we passing the knowledge to the industry players and building managers to help them ease into the new regulations?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How much is it expected to cost them?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And will it ultimately lead to a significant increase in rent or overheads?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These business costs are still important to consider as they ultimately lead to a higher cost for end consumers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: At the national level, I think NEA has done a good job in tackling food waste.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: First, by working with schools to cultivate our students with good habits.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Second are the ongoing campaigns, such as "Love your Food.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Save More." But the reality is that tackling the root of the food issue means reducing all this food waste in the first place.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today, we stroll through our social media feeds and we inevitably see posts of glorious food at hashtag foodporn.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, we could also start posting our empty plates with the hashtag "SG don't waste food".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe that this significant increase in collection points nationwide will surely yield better recycling rates for e-waste.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In preparation for this speech, I researched on some information regarding food waste in Singapore, particularly at the NEA website.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And like Members who have spoken before me, I do find the food waste situation very worrying.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And this is expected to increase further with our growing population, economic activity and affluence.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Despite earlier efforts to promote conservation of food, food waste is still mounting year by year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In other words, the main bulk of our unconsumed food ends up mostly in our usual rubbish trash and is eventually sent for incineration.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whether from the food resource optimisation or from public health standpoint, the current state of affairs on food waste is not sustainable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are not doing justice to our precious food source.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am glad that the Government is making policy moves now to reduce and manage food waste.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my view, the key contributing factor to this situation is, firstly, the lack of awareness to prevent and reduce food waste at its source; and secondly, the lack of food waste treatment infrastructure in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The approach is to initially target commercial and industrial buildings that generate large amounts of food waste, such as large hotels, malls, as well as industrial facilities that house food manufacturers and caterers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I agree with this approach, as a start, essentially focusing on the big food waste generators where it can move the needle in terms of food waste recycling.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While I support these new measures, I would also like to ask the Minister how difficult it would be for the businesses to implement these regulations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Are the costs likely to be very high to the businesses?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can I also ask if there are already existing premises that adopt food segregation practices onsite?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are the results and benefits so far?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, how successful have we been in recovering energy from food waste?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond expanding the practice to the industrial and commercial spaces, does the Government intend to expand the practice of recycling food to residential areas as well?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Back to my first point with regard to the lack of awareness in the area of prevention and reduction of food waste, I strongly believe that more can be done.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I read in some studies that, on average, about one-third of all the food produced for human consumption is not consumed but actually wasted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not only a waste of money for businesses and consumers, but it is also costing the earth and worsening global warming.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When food is wasted, even more food is needed to be produced to meet the demand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Consequently, the resources used to cultivate, deliver and distribute the food will also go to waste.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Every one of us contributes to this wastage in some way: the food producers, the food businesses, as well as all of us individually – the consumers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have read about the many ways and ideas how we could reduce food waste.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure we will continue to come up with and discover more new ways.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, with the advent of technology and data, we should leverage more digital means to better match the supply and production of food with the demand and consumption of food.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, there is over production of food due to misreading or misjudging consumer demand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If there are more digital channels to place order for food, mobile apps to plan our meals and so on, businesses and producers would be able to better right-size their production and reduce food wastage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hopefully, this could lead to cost reductions, possibly benefiting consumers when there is sufficient competition.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we can reduce food waste as a major thrust of our efforts, it is half the battle won.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The other half of the battle would be to look at how we can reuse and recycle the food where possible.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cutting food waste requires both system and regulatory changes, as well as lifestyle and cultural changes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, mooncake was just mentioned by Members, as we tend to give and receive multiple boxes of mooncakes from one another.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is really a waste in most cases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, the 10-course dinners that we have – do we really need an eight- or 10-course dinner?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, it would lead to more food waste, as well as over consumption – both undesirable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Earlier in the year, I read in the news about this year-long drive as part of the Towards Zero Waste campaign where consumers are encouraged at food outlets to, firstly, order what we eat; secondly, ask for less rice or noodle if unable to eat that much; and thirdly, say "no" to side dishes that we will not consume.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While I applaud this worthy initiative, I have not seen this message reaching out to enough people.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I need to apologise that after the Member talked about the 10-course dinner, Members would have to wait for a little while more.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The questions posed by Members in many ways mirror the deliberations and considerations in our design of the regulatory framework.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: On the one hand, doing more and moving faster will allow us to better care for the environment as the threat of climate change is ever-growing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members like Mr Louis Ng and Ms Anthea Ong have given various ideas that we can consider moving forward.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: On the other hand, we need to be mindful of costs to businesses and consumers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As highlighted by Members Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Douglas Foo, Dr Teo Ho Pin, Mr Henry Kwek and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, operating and compliance costs are key concerns for businesses, more so as we enter a period of slowing economic growth.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, we have adopted a pragmatic approach to achieve our environmental goals, while managing the impact on businesses and consumers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many gave us useful inputs which we have incorporated.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, to minimise the reporting burden, NEA will centralise all reporting and submission of documents on one common online platform.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will also develop online reporting templates and audit procedures that will streamline processes and reduce the manpower needed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In response to industry feedback, we have built in greater flexibility in the implementation of these regulations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, producers of non-consumer Electrical and Electronic Equipment (EEE) can collect unwanted products from their customers within a reasonable amount of time after receiving their requests, instead of doing so immediately.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The same flexibility is also given to retailers in providing the free one-for-one collection service when they deliver products to the customers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, we have sought to minimise regulatory impact on smaller businesses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Third, we have sought to keep our regulatory framework consistent with other jurisdictions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, our e-waste EPR framework has incorporated best practices adapted from the systems in Sweden and South Korea and is customised to suit Singapore's context.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many of the companies which will be covered by this Bill also have global presence, including in countries where EPR is implemented.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will allow them to adjust more easily to our EPR system and minimise business costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Fourth, we will provide sufficient time and support for companies to adjust.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Mr Desmond Choo has suggested, we will stagger the timeline for the regulatory requirements to come into effect.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also working with industry associations to educate and assist companies with the mandatory reporting requirements for packaging waste and the implementation of their 3R plans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, NEA has co-funded 24 onsite food waste treatment systems at premises, such as Parkway Parade, Resorts World Sentosa and InterContinental Singapore Robertson Quay, under its 3R Fund.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Fifth, our regulatory framework must support the development of the Environmental Services Industry to take advantage of the circular economy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides ensuring environmental and resource sustainability, this will allow us to maximise economic benefits by developing the local recycling industry and allowing our companies to export their solutions overseas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At the same time, greater economies of scale and the development of new solutions will help to bring down costs at the systems level.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: According to a 2015 study by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and McKinsey, adopting a circular economy approach could boost Europe's resource productivity by 3% by 2030 and generate cost savings of €600 billion a year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Another 2015 study by the UK's Waste and Resources Action Programme found that a circular economy has the potential to create 1.2 to three million jobs in the continent by 2030.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We believe that the Resource Sustainability Bill will open up new economic opportunities for Singapore companies and Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With these measures, we expect that companies will be able to cope with the new regulations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similarly, as Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Anthea Ong have asked, we do not expect the cost that may be passed down to customers to be significant.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A study on the EU's EPR on Waste EEE showed that the average increase in the prices of products was about 2% after the regulation was introduced, a small fraction of the cost of the product.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Producers are unlikely to raise the retail prices of their products significantly, as this will affect their price competitiveness.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Moreover, as we aggregate such waste streams and extract value from them, there is potential to bring down costs at the systems level.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will now address specific points of clarification raised by Members on the three waste streams.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the current e-waste collection and recycling landscape in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is why we are putting in place a formal EPR framework to ensure that e-waste is properly collected and recycled.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Desmond Choo asked about the thresholds and coverage of producers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As I have explained earlier, we have sought to minimise regulatory impact on our SMEs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The threshold levels have thus been set to cover about 90% of regulated products that are put-to-market by weight.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The remaining 10% of regulated products are sold by small producers with small individual market shares.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will monitor the implementation of the EPR framework and ensure that these thresholds remain relevant.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin, Mr Christopher de Souza, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Henry Kwek asked how the regulatory measures will affect e-commerce in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The regulations will cover all Singapore-registered producers, regardless of the channels through which they conduct their business.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, laptops which Apple sells in Singapore through its online store will count towards its put-to-market tonnage.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similarly, retailers are obligated to offer a free one-for-one takeback when they deliver a product of the same type, even if the product is sold online.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, it is difficult to impose our regulations on overseas suppliers of EEE.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is a challenge faced around the world, including established EPR systems in the EU.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will closely monitor developments in this area and consult the local industry further on ways to bring overseas suppliers on board.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nonetheless, Members may be reassured that all consumers will have access to proper e-waste collection and recycling channels, regardless of where they buy their electronic products from.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This includes the network of collection points set up by the PRS operator, and contacting the PRS operator directly for takeback.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We welcome companies not covered by the regulatory framework to partner with the appointed PRS operator to conduct e-waste collection programmes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how the e-waste collection targets are set.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The collection targets set by NEA are based on percentage of consumer products put-to-market by weight.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These targets were determined based on consumer e-waste disposal patterns in Singapore and referenced targets set by the EU in the early stages of their EPR implementation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will monitor the amount of e-waste collected and adjust the collection targets accordingly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As the EPR system is new, we will start off with lower targets and scale them up as the system matures.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over time, we will aspire towards the 65% e-waste collection targets set by the EU for all product categories.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is because the PRS operator will need time to build up their infrastructure and collection network to optimise collection, as well as raise awareness of the producers and consumers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even in the EU, which Mr Louis Ng has cited, member states were given a few years to meet their targets.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the role that the informal sector will play to support the regulatory framework.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As individuals are not regulated under the Resource Sustainability Bill, the rag-and-bone or karang guni men will be allowed to continue in their trade and collect unwanted EEE products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, NEA is seeking to integrate the informal sector into the e-waste collection network that will be established by the PRS operator.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is important given that waste, particularly e-waste, contains hazardous substances and needs to be disposed of in a proper manner.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The tender documents for the PRS operator will specify that applicants must demonstrate an understanding of how the informal sector currently operates, and develop a plan to integrate them into the collection networks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, the PRS operator could conduct training for the karang guni men or engage them as logistics providers in the collection network.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The appointed PRS operator must follow through with their plans as part of their licencing conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also asked about the management of unwanted personal mobility devices (PMDs) in view of the policy to disallow the use of non-UL2272 certified PMDs on public paths from July 2020.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is supporting the Land Transport Authority (LTA) to develop solutions to allow the public to dispose of unwanted PMDs safely and conveniently, and to ensure the collected PMDs are properly recycled.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is assisting LTA with the setting up of designated PMD collection points.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When the Bill comes into effect, we will require all producers of PMDs to join PRS.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also rightly highlighted the importance of growing our local e-waste recycling capabilities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently, there is sufficient recycling capacity for information and communications technology equipment and televisions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singapore faces limitations in recycling large appliances, such as refrigerators and washing machines.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The EPR framework will play a pivotal role in developing the recycling industry, by financing and driving the demand for recycling services, and by aggregating e-waste into more viable volumes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will encourage entrepreneurs to enter the market and set up recycling plants and facilities in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Several recyclers, both local and overseas, have indicated interest to expand or set up facilities to recycle large household appliances, batteries and lamps.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has been working with the relevant agencies to support these interested companies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The development of our local recycling industry will not just allow Singapore to meet our recycling needs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Mr Desmond Choo has pointed out, it has the potential to create economic opportunities and good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Take TES Singapore, a local e-waste recycler which has expanded to more than 30 locations worldwide, as an example.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: TES Singapore is currently building a new facility to treat lithium-ion batteries from electric vehicles, which is a covered product subjected to EPR under the Bill.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As the treatment process involves chemical extraction, new jobs for engineers with specialised skills in this field will be created.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More importantly, it will drive resource sustainability by incentivising producers to redesign their products to last longer and for easier recycling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This helps shift mindsets towards the circular economy approach and sustainable consumption, which Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Christopher de Souza have both emphasised the importance of.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under this framework, companies that import packaged products or use packaging in the course of their business, will be required to submit their packaging data and their plans to reduce, reuse or recycle to NEA.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This covers all packaging introduced along the supply chain, from manufacturing to repackaging, to door-to-door delivery and the point of sale.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Packaging introduced by Singapore-registered companies through online platforms to the consumer market will also be captured.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Dennis Tan asked how this threshold was determined.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As I have explained in my opening speech, the threshold has been set at more than $10 million in annual turnover for a start, to minimise the impact on micro and small enterprises.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Ong Teng Koon asked if we should introduce reduction targets for packaging waste, including penalties for non-compliance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our approach is to allow companies the flexibility to set their own targets for their 3R plans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach, as the use of packaging is dynamic and varies across sectors and companies, which Mr Henry Kwek has also highlighted.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Companies may have different approaches in implementing 3R initiatives which can help them save on costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They also need time to build up their capability.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is also why we will not penalise companies for failure to fulfil their plans, but instead recognise those who do well and share best practices to level up all companies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will support companies in developing their 3R plans to reduce, reuse and recycle packaging.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is working with companies which have successfully implemented 3R initiatives under the Singapore Packaging Agreement to come up with best practices, potential initiatives and key performance indicators (KPIs) to aid companies in developing their 3R plans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is also working with the industry to develop a capability-building programme for companies that will include the sharing of best practices and recognition for companies’ zero waste efforts, which were also suggested by Mr Henry Kwek and Prof Lim Sun Sun.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also building up our local plastics recycling capability to better extract resources from plastic waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our vision is to close the plastic waste loop locally where feasible, especially given the tightening restrictions on the transboundary movement of recyclables which various Members have highlighted.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is currently studying recycling solutions and technologies, and assessing their suitability for adoption in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, this includes mechanical recycling to turn plastic waste into plastic pellets for manufacturing new products, or chemical recycling to turn plastic waste into chemical feedstock or fuel.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will go hand-in-hand with the EPR framework for packaging waste that we will establish no later than 2025.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The recycling facilities will allow Singapore to turn our plastic waste into higher value products locally, while the EPR will consolidate and ensure sufficient feedstock for the plants to operate in an economically viable manner.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will now address the points raised by Members on the mandatory segregation and treatment of food waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the type of buildings that will be covered under this framework.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is currently conducting food waste audits at commercial and industrial premises with food establishments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The information gathered from these audits will help determine the thresholds for large food waste generators.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the benefits of onsite segregation and treatment of food waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While there are costs associated with the installation of onsite food waste treatment systems, businesses are able to reap cost savings from reduced waste disposal costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, there are other benefits, such as a cleaner environment, increased value of dry recyclables due to less contamination by food waste, and potential resources generated through the treatment process.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about the options to treat food waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Food waste can be converted into biogas and compost.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Both are useful products and the choice would depend on factors, such as the availability of off-takers and economies of scale.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Liang Eng Hwa have asked if the mandatory segregation and treatment of food waste will be onerous for building managers to implement.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have worked closely with relevant stakeholders in developing the food waste measures and will continue to support them in their implementation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To help the industry better understand and comply with the requirements, NEA has published on its website a list of possible onsite food waste treatment systems that companies can consider using.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Building managers of existing premises also have the flexibility to choose the treatment solution that best suits their operations, including offsite treatment at the upcoming Tuas Nexus.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to adopt relevant learning points from successful food waste segregation policies in overseas jurisdictions, such as EU member states, Japan and Taiwan, that focus on requiring businesses to segregate food waste for separate collection.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is consistent with the practices in most other jurisdictions, such as the EU and Japan, where food waste segregation and treatment measures are targeted primarily at commercial and industrial premises.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nonetheless, we will continue to work with the community to identify suitable opportunities to reduce and recycle food waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As mentioned by Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Miss Cheng Li Hui, NEA has been actively promoting the reduction of food waste generation at source through campaigns and engagements in the communities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As NEA's campaign tagline says: "Let's buy, order or cook just enough!" Mr Douglas Foo highlighted NEA's series of food waste minimisation guidebooks for food retail establishments, supermarkets and food manufacturing establishments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similarly, we have also developed a "Guide to Implementing Environmentally-friendly Best Practices for Events" for the public sector to reduce food waste, as suggested by Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This guide has been shared with public agencies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to work with them to encourage adoption of the best practices when organising events.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The guidebooks share best practices and highlight technologies, such as smart bins that can measure, identify and track food waste through sensors and image recognition technology.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: One such system was developed by a Singapore startup, Good for Food, which Mr Louis Ng and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira mentioned.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We should also learn from countries, such as the US, Canada and Italy, which have implemented such laws.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our approach will have to strike a balance between managing food waste and ensuring that any food donated is safe for consumption, particularly in our tropical climate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Resource Sustainability Bill is a big stride that the Government has taken to catalyse the transition to a circular economy and enhance our climate, resource and economic resiliences.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Tackling climate change in a resource-constrained future is such a massive challenge that our fight needs bigger weapons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The shift from a voluntary to mandatory approach in ensuring resource sustainability is not something that the Government takes lightly, but only after careful consideration and consultation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We need businesses, organisations and individuals to come on board with innovative and effective solutions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are, therefore, heartened that many businesses here have taken the lead to implement circular solutions in their value chain.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Fuji Xerox, for example, has adopted a closed-loop system where parts and materials are recovered and reused.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This has allowed Fuji Xerox to save around 30% of new materials used in manufacturing their products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nestlé Singapore has saved 2,000 tonnes of packaging used for its MILO® products by changing the packaging design and optimising production practices.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Not only is this good for the environment, it has also helped Nestlé Singapore to reduce business costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also seeing more packaging-free grocery stores, such as UnPackt.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These stores encourage customers to bring their own containers and allow them to buy what they need instead of a prepackaged amount.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They also offer more competitive prices, as going without packaging has reduced the cost of products by some 10%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: FairPrice Vivocity, the largest FairPrice store in Singapore, now offers packaging-free grains, nuts, spices and pasta for shoppers to buy loose quantities of these products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is probably the "nude" zone that Mr Louis Ng is recommending supermarkets to have.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are encouraged by these efforts and welcome more businesses to embrace such practices and go "nude".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are harnessing the strength of our youths and community partners to co-create solutions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since March this year, MEWR, together with the National Youth Council, has been engaging our youth leaders on our environmental policies and programmes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Through their lens, we hope to better understand youth perspectives on climate change, environment and sustainability issues and empower them to lead ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, the Climate SG Alliance, formed by 18 corporates, educational and civil society leaders, has been promoting education in schools on waste minimisation and educating the community on recycling right.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MEWR will also convene a Citizens' Workgroup, comprising Singaporeans from diverse backgrounds, to co-create solutions that will improve the way we recycle at home.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The #RecycleRight Workgroup will kick off its first session on 21 September and we are looking forward to the ideas from the Workgroup.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also keen to co-create solutions to tackle the excessive consumption of single-use plastics.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I believe this is an issue that has seized the hearts and minds of many Singaporeans, including, of course, Members of this House.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have been monitoring how other countries manage their single-use plastics.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many have adopted regulatory measures to curb the generation of plastic waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Plastic bag charges in jurisdictions, such as Hong Kong, Ireland, the UK and the Netherlands, have, indeed, shown a reduction in consumption of plastic bags.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singapore's approach to addressing excessive consumption of single-use plastics, such as plastic bags, needs to take into account our unique urbanised, high-rise living context.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Most of the plastic bags that Singaporeans bring home from the shops and supermarkets are not "single-use".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We reuse them for other purposes, such as carrying wet items, before eventually using them to bag waste for disposal.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This has become a way of life for Singaporeans and ensured that our waste disposal is clean and hygienic.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All our waste, including plastics, are safely incinerated.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, they do not cause the landfill problem that many other countries which are reliant on landfills suffer from.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, a single-use plastic bag that is used for, maybe 30 minutes, as some say, but will be left in the landfill for more than 30 years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We remove any litter that enters our waterways with litter traps and flotsam removal craft and conduct beach and underwater clean-ups.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All these measures prevent any litter, including plastics, from ending up in the sea and contributing to marine pollution.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We all share the goal of tackling climate change and protecting our environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nevertheless, Singaporeans have expressed differing views on how to deal with single-use plastics.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For now, the majority of Singaporeans seem to prefer an educational approach to encourage people to consume less.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Government will continue to engage the community and businesses and listen to their views and feedback.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The announcement has elicited strong reactions on social media.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We urge Members of this House and the public to support NTUC FairPrice and the trial.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I encourage other major supermarket chains, like Dairy Farm, Sheng Siong and Prime to do their part, too.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The insights gained could also help inform recommendations made by the proposed Workgroup.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will consider all options and I welcome Members to share your views and ideas, too.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will allow us to use our resources and grow our economy sustainably.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will also catalyse innovative circular business models and position our companies to seize opportunities in the region and beyond for waste treatment, recycling or remanufacturing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While change can be catalysed strategically at the level of businesses, community and civic organisations, our individual efforts are important, too.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We can all make small changes in our daily lives and contribute to protecting our environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, let us all be part of the solution to secure our collective future.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: They also use the plastic bag to bag their trash.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I do not think we can keep using that argument.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We also just said that we will support NTUC FairPrice for introducing a plastic bag charge.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But, at the same time, we keep giving reasons why it is not going to work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I just hope we can have a single stand on whether we support the plastic bag charge or we do not support the plastic bag charge.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I think I have just given the Member the information, particularly on the survey that shows that we do have differing views on this issue of single-use plastics, whether to charge for plastic bags or not.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I have also given the Member in detail the various reasons why our context is unique.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, it is not an excuse that we do not want to charge for plastic bags but because people are reusing them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Let us work together and come to an inclusive solution on the way forward.
